# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-22 (Extended v163)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826; **current narrative point (evening of 24th June 1832, Lamarque's funeral rioting)**: Primary locations include Paris—Rue Plumet (Valjean's house), Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, ruin wall, Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire No. 6 (Gillenormand residence), Champ-de-Mars, Austerlitz bridge, Quai Bourdon, Boulevard Bourdon, Rue Bassompierre, Isle Louviers timber-yards, Arsenal, Marais, Rue du Pont-aux-Choux, Rue de Thorigny, Rue Ponceau, numerous barricaded streets across Paris. English provincial towns (Ravenmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Staveford, Gulhaven, Kelmere, Kelford, Pontoise). **Seasonal progression**: Winter Year 5 transitioned to spring Year 6 (cholera), now summer Year 6 evening of 24th June 1832. **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Yera Stenworth confided fire at Dunstead granary set deliberately—unverified. **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Fenelle Lindmere confided Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family—unverified. **Unverified claim (mid-June 1832)**: In letter Ferald burned after reading, Marald revealed Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family.

## Jean Valjean and Cosette (through evening 24th June 1832)
**The wound**: Day following Jondrette visit, Valjean appeared with large inflamed wound on left arm resembling burn. Detained one month with fever; refused doctor. Cosette devoted herself to care. Recovered through March-April.

**Mysterious journeys and nocturnal manuscript**: Valjean took occasional journeys, destination unknown. Found carrying large club in garden dusk. Cosette discovered philosophical manuscript on bench—meditation on love as divine spark. **Recognized writer as Marius.**

**Imminent departure (late June 1832)**: Morning of 24th June, Valjean told Cosette he must settle affairs; she must hold herself in readiness; linen to pack; obliged to go on journey; all to be ready in one week. **Possible destination: England.**

**Thénardier sighting**: Caught sight of Thénardier in disguise (workman's waistcoat, gray linen trousers, cap) while walking on boulevard during spring Year 6. Since that day, has seen him repeatedly; certain Thénardier prowling neighborhood. Now rarely goes out with Cosette; spends time meditating on isolated slopes of Champ-de-Mars.

**Mysterious figure (spring Year 6)**: Perceived creature larger than child, not so large as man, clad in gray blouse and dust-colored cotton velvet trousers, jumping over parapet and slipping into moat. Identity unclear.

**Political unease**: Paris not tranquil; police uneasy and suspicious. Valjean fears discovery as man like himself might be readily apprehended.

## Marius and Cosette's Romance (through evening 24th June 1832)
**Recognition and revelation**: Upon reading manuscript, Cosette acknowledged she had never forgotten Marius, had always loved him. "Fire had been smothered, and had smouldered for a time," but now "it burst forth afresh, and inflamed her whole being."

**Garden encounter and nature of love**: Beginning autumn Year 5, Marius came every evening. Entered garden by forcing old gate. **At height of love's voluptuousness, Marius remained absolutely chaste.** Love described as "chaste, almost shy" yet not devoid of gallantry. Conversations made of breaths, murmurs, whispers, childish prattle, laughter.

**Confessions of identity (spring Year 6)**: **Cholera decimated Paris during that month.** **Marius told Cosette**: orphan, name Marius Pontmercy, lawyer, lived by writing for publishers, father was colonel and hero, on bad terms with rich grandfather, hinted at being baron. **Cosette told Marius**: brought up at Petit-Picpus convent, mother dead, father's name M. Fauchelevent, very good, gave greatly to poor.

**Marius's response and last arrangement (late June 1832)**: For last six weeks, Marius slowly taken possession of Cosette. **Upon learning of Valjean's plan to take Cosette to England in one week**: Marius declared this gravest atrocity imaginable. **Protested he has no money (owes more than ten louis to Courfeyrac), old hat, coat missing buttons, shirt ragged, elbows torn, boots leak, cannot afford passport.** Cosette agreed not to question further. **Arranged to meet in garden day after tomorrow (26th June) at nine o'clock at dusk.**

**Marius's despair (evening 24th June 1832)**: Approached grating to garden. Displaced bar and rushed headlong in. Cosette not at waiting spot. Traversed thicket, approached recess—not there. Raised eyes; shutters closed. Made tour of garden; deserted. Returned to house and knocked repeatedly, called "Cosette!" imperiously. No reply. **Fixed despairing eyes on dismal house, black and silent as tomb. Seated himself on flight of steps, heart filled with sweetness and resolution. Blessed his love, said to himself that since Cosette was gone, all that was left for him was to die.**

**Marius carries pistols (spring Year 6 through summer Year 6)**: Took pistols Javert gave him at time of 3d February adventure; they remained loaded. Summer Year 6: Put pistols in pocket and went out with Enjolras, Feuilly, and Combeferre, all ready to go out. Vague thought when taking them unclear.

## Father Gillenormand (through evening 24th June 1832)
**Character**: Well past ninety-first birthday. Lives with Mademoiselle Gillenormand in Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, No. 6. Incapable of taking single step towards grandson. Placed old portrait of dead daughter opposite head of bed—gazed incessantly at it.

**Evening of 24th June 1832 (before Marius's arrival)**: Alone in chamber, feet on andirons, half enveloped in coromandel lacquer screen, thinking of Marius lovingly and bitterly; bitterness predominated.

**Marius's arrival and interrogation**: Gillenormand grasped Marius at glance. Found him noble, handsome, distinguished. Desired to embrace him, but harshness came forth instead. Delivered bitter diatribe. **Announced he would marry.** Upon learning her name related to Fauchelevent, declared absolutely: "Never, sir, never!"

**Sudden reversal and Marius's confession**: At tone of "never," Marius lost hope, traversed chamber tottering. At moment of exit, Gillenormand advanced with senile vivacity, seized him by collar, flung him into armchair with kindness and paternal warmth. **Marius passionately declared love for Cosette, described meeting her at Luxembourg, seeing her every day, her father's planned departure to England, his desperation without her.** Stated: "She lives in a garden with an iron fence, in the Rue Plumet. It is in the neighborhood of the Invalides."

**Gillenormand's dangerous response and misrecognition (late June 1832)**: Seated near table while listening and drinking snuff. **At words "Rue Plumet" Gillenormand interrupted his inhalation and allowed remainder of snuff to fall upon his knees.** **Delivered rambling response containing reference to "Rue Blomet, Pamela, barracks, lancer," which passed before Marius like dissolving view.** **Terminated rambling in words which Marius understood as mortal insult to Cosette: "make her your mistress."** **Those words entered heart of strict young man like sword.** Octogenarian raised hands to temples with anguish, recoiled, fell back into armchair, pulseless, voiceless, tearless, quivering head, lips moving with stupid air. **However, Marius was at age when one believes nothing in line of evil. Suspicions are wrinkles; early youth has none. Suspect Cosette! Marius could sooner have committed crimes. Gillenormand's dangerous mischaracterization left no trace in Marius's mind; not slightest.**

## Éponine's Guardianship (Spring Year 6)
**Éponine guards Rue Plumet house against intruders.** On evening of 3d June 1832, towards ten o'clock, confronts unknown parties: tells them she is there; forbids entry; claims she is dog and will bark; says six men don't frighten her; threatens kicks; displays resolute attitude.

## Thénardier's Escape and Accomplices (Winter Year 5)
**Escape from Prison Chargemagne**: At two o'clock morning, old sentinel relieved by conscript. At four o'clock, relieving sentinel found conscript asleep. **Thénardier vanished. Hole in cage ceiling. Bed plank wrenched off. Half-empty bottle with stupefying wine seized. Soldier's bayonet disappeared.** Reached edge of ruin wall but strength failed.

**Four ruffians' vigil and Gavroche's role**: Brujon, Guelemer, Babet, and Montparnasse prowled all night around La Force. **Guelemer seized Gavroche, set him on roof of shanty, handed him rope knotted by Brujon. Gavroche directed steps towards flue. Thénardier bent over wall edge; first light of dawn struck white upon his sweat-dripping brow. Gavroche recognized him.** Brujon and Guelemer successfully escaped.

## Gavroche (Spring Year 6—Evening 24th June 1832)
**Character and activities**: Street child, homeless, hungry, clever pickpocket. Gamin of letters—apprenticed three months to printer, executed commission for M. Baour-Lormian (one of the Forty). Well up in popular tunes; combines repertory of birds with repertory of workshops; acquainted with thieves.

**Two lost children and elephant shelter (Spring Year 6)**: Observed two neatly dressed children. Provided bread and promised shelter. Led two children through fence gap into elephant enclosure. All three sheltered inside elephant through winter Year 5. **Hair-dresser who chased children from his shop during this period**: Now (evening 24th June) engaged in shaving old Empire soldier in his shop, discussing riot and Lamarque.

**Evening of 24th June 1832 activities**: Armed with pistol (source unclear). Arrived at Rue du Pont-aux-Choux pistol in hand. Found only pastry-cook's shop open; attempted to purchase apple-turnover but had no money; shouted "Help!" Without resistance, picked up fallen lancer's horse on pavement, assisted in raising it, then resumed way with pistol. In Rue de Thorigny, all was peace and silence. **At hair-dresser's shop on Rue de Thorigny**: Unable to resist impulse to say good day to proprietor (the hair-dresser who had chased the children); flung stone through panes, then fled at full speed towards Marché Saint-Jean. Spoke defiantly of fighting despotism, enduring rheumatism, giving days to country.

## Lamarque's Funeral Procession and Ensuing Riots (Mid-June 1832—Evening 24th June)
**General Lamarque**: Man of renown and action. Had bravery of Empire and Restoration. Eloquent as valiant. Beloved of people because served Emperor well. One of Napoleon's marshals with Comtes Gérard and Drouet. For seventeen years majestically preserved sadness of Waterloo. In death agony clasped sword to breast. Died mid-June 1832 uttering word "country."

**Government military response**: Four squadrons carabineers, Municipal Guard, dragoons, Light Infantry, artillery prepared. Power uneasy, held suspended twenty-four thousand soldiers in city and thirty thousand in banlieue.

**Funeral procession and dragoon intervention (mid-June 1832)**: Procession proceeded from deceased's house via boulevards to Bastille. At Bastille, long files from Faubourg Saint-Antoine effected junction. **Lafayette spoke and bade Lamarque farewell. Touching and august instant, all heads uncovered, all hearts beat high.** Red flag raised, disappeared. Shouts: "Lamarque to the Pantheon!—Lafayette to the Town-hall!" Young men began dragging hearse across Austerlitz bridge. **Three shots suddenly discharged: first killed Cholet, chief of squadron; second killed old deaf woman closing her window; third singed shoulder of officer.** Squadron of dragoons debouted at gallop with bared swords through streets, sweeping all before them.

**Generalizing of riots (evening 24th June 1832)**: At instant when insurrection started movement in procession, frightful ebb ensued. Great river of crowd covering boulevards divided; rout scattered; all ran, fled, escaped with shouts of attack or pallor of flight. Crowd overflowed right and left, spread in torrents over two hundred streets with roar of broken sewer. Tempest loosed, stones rained, fusillade broke forth. Timber-yards of Isle Louviers bristled with combatants. Stakes torn up, barricade begun. Young men thrust back hearse at run.

**Spontaneous uprising across Paris**: Nothing more extraordinary than first breaking out of riot. Everything burst forth everywhere at once. Shops closed. Red flags and proclamations carried. Factory of small-arms pillaged; three armorers' shops plundered. Young men armed with muskets installed themselves in houses to fire from windows. Across right bank, left bank, quays, boulevards, Latin country, quarter of Halles: panting men, artisans, students broke street lanterns, unpaved streets, broke doors, uprooted trees, rummaged cellars, heaped paving-stones, furniture, planks, made barricades. Forced bourgeois to assist. Wrote on doors: "The arms have been delivered." Disarmed sentinels and National Guardsmen. Tore epaulets from officers.

**Barricade construction (mid-June 1832)**: In less than an hour, twenty-seven barricades sprang out of earth in quarter of Halles alone. Famous house No. 50 was fortress, commanded three streets, flanked by barricades. Without reckoning innumerable barricades in twenty other quarters—Marais, Mont-Sainte-Geneviève, porte-cochère torn from hinges, carriage overthrown near Hôtel-Dieu.

**Organization and command**: At barricade of Rue des Ménétriers, well-dressed man distributed money to workmen. At Rue Grenetat, horseman handed roll of silver to commander. Light-haired young man without cravat went from barricade to barricade carrying pass-words. Another with naked sword and blue police cap placed sentinels. Wine-shops and porters' lodges converted into guard-houses. Riot conducted after scientific military tactics. Narrow, uneven, sinuous streets full of angles and turns admirably chosen. Society of the Friends of the People undertaken to direct insurrection in Quartier Sainte-Avoye. Man killed in Rue du Ponceau searched had plan of Paris on person.

**Direction of uprising**: That which really undertaken direction was strange impetuosity in air. Insurrection built barricades with one hand, seized nearly all posts of garrison with other. In less than three hours, insurgents invaded and occupied: right bank—Arsenal, Mayoralty of Place Royale, Marais, Popincourt arms manufactory, la Galiote, Château-d'Eau, streets near Halles; left bank—barracks of Veterans, Sainte-Pélagie, Place Maubert, powder magazine of Deux-Moulins, all barriers. At five o'clock evening, masters of Bastille, Lingerie, Blancs-Manteaux; scouts reached Place des Victoires, menaced Bank, Petits-Pères barracks, Post-Office. **A third of Paris in hands of rioters.**

**Evening and night (24th June 1832)**: Evening came, theatres did not open; patrols circulated with irritation; passers-by searched; suspicious persons arrested. By nine o'clock, more than eight hundred persons arrested. Call to arms beaten, National Guard armed in haste, legions emerged from Mayoralities, regiments from barracks. Drummer received blow from dagger; another assailed by thirty young men, another killed. Three officers fell dead one after another. Many Municipal Guards, on being wounded, retreated. Saint-Merry tocsin began. Marshal Soult regarded with gloomy air. Long vault called Rue de Paris littered with straw and prisoners. Prisoners slept in open air in meadows, piled on each other. Men sprang up at corners shouting "Go home!" People bolted doors. Paris seemed to take on more mournful hue from formidable flaming of revolt.

## Provincial Details (Winter Year 5—Summer Year 6)
Deaths, transfers, births, migrations: Ulrald Corrford died of old age at Staveford. Kassa Stenson gave work as scribe. Yewyn Haskick gave birth to son Sebin Brackick; father Tatho Brackick; family in Salcombe. Rovus Prydenridge quit Ostcombe for Kelmere. Wenelle Lindmere went to live in Kelmere. **Summer Year 6**: Volia Brackick died of drowning in flood, laid in churchyard at Kelford. Volan Stenworth laughed at story nobody else found funny; walked long way round to avoid muddy square; watched clouds and predicted rain wrongly; counted coins twice, came up penny short. Isvie Stenworth spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight. Ferald laughed at story nobody else found funny. Lurald laughed at story nobody else found funny. Movie Prydenridge and Zavus Prydenridge talked of weather, harvest, lame horse. Jotho Thornmere remarked river is up again; Nerine Prydenridge said it always was in spring. Yera hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step. Fenelle Lindmere hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step. Smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; bees hummed in lavender. Wind came off water with smell of salt and tar. Children chased hoop down lane shrieking. Someone chalked crooked sun on wall of forge. Gulls quarreled over heap of fish heads by steps. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. **Kelford harbor town**: Rag-picker tradition—humble figure who sorts basket contents systematically into categories (rags, cores, stalks, linen, woollen stuff, papers, food, glass, shoes, bones).

## M. Mabeuf's Destitution (Spring Year 6—4th June 1832)
**Character and losses**: Venerable old man of austerity and learning. Received Jean Valjean's purse (from Gavroche) but in infantile austerity took it to police commissioner as lost article. Forced to sell library volume by volume for pittance. Belonged to Horticultural Society; destitution became known. Attended dinner with Minister; no one spoke to him. Perceived ragged cravat and waxed shoes astonished ushers.

**Final sacrifice (4th June 1832)**: Mother Plutarque fell ill; needed expensive potion and nurse. Only Diogenes Laertius remained in bookcase. Put unique copy under arm, sold it, returned with one hundred francs. Laid pile of five-franc pieces on serving-woman's nightstand, returned without saying word. Seated himself on overturned post in garden at dawn, motionless over hedge, head drooping, eyes vaguely fixed on withered flower-beds. Rained at intervals; old man did not perceive.
